en: The Scripture on the Buddha’s Explanation for the Brahmin Āṣāḍha, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī together with five hundred śramaṇas.
He arrived at the city of Drumavastu and sat beneath a tree outside the walls.

At that time, there was a prominent and virtuous brahmin in the vicinity named Pukkasa, who was profoundly learned in the scriptures and the movements of the stars and constellations, and could answer whatever questions were posed to him.
He had five hundred disciples, the foremost among whom was named Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya.
Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya asked his teacher, saying:
"Now there is a Buddha who has come; people extol his virtue, and his fame covers heaven and earth. I do not know who this person is."
Vaiśravaṇa said: "I have heard that this is the crown prince of the Śākya kings, who attained his awakening without a teacher and has composed sūtras for the sake of transformation. Aśvaghoṣa said:
"If he had no teacher, how could his reputation be so magnificent?

Furthermore, as a prince, he was surely full of arrogance, lust, and fondness for pleasure; how could he have been willing to travel on foot, humble his will, beg for food, and tirelessly instruct others?"
"Could this be a true man!
I wish for you, Master, to go and observe his virtue and conduct. Pukkasāti said:

"No," he replied, "I am a man of noble lineage and distinguished virtue, wise and possessed of many talents. He is but newly emerged; it is right that he come to pay his respects to me, and it is not fitting for me to go to him.

Āṣāḍha said, "I have heard that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the seventh Brahmā both descend to serve him. His disciples, under his instruction, all attain the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*): they can levitate and fly, see through walls and hear through solid objects, know the thoughts of others, and discern where beings have come from in their past lives and where they will go after death."
"This is surely the Celestial Master; how could he deign to come and visit! Piṅgiya said:

"The scriptures state that when a king fathers a son who possesses the thirty-two marks, he shall immediately become a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), ruling over the four quarters of the world. Seven natural treasures will appear: first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth, the jade woman treasure; fifth, the divine jewel treasure; sixth, the steward treasure; and seventh, the wise general treasure. He shall have a thousand sons, all talented, brilliant, brave, and martial—each man equal to a thousand others. Weapons shall not be used, and the world shall be in great peace."
"If he abandons the world, he shall become a Buddha of spontaneity (*ziran*), using non-action (*wuwei*) as his transformation, delivering people so they may attain the Way. Could it be him?
You should go and observe."
"One who possesses these marks must surely be the Buddha;
I shall serve him. Āṣāḍha said, "I wish to go together with my companions."
The Master said, "Very well.
He then went together with five hundred disciples; upon arrival, they all alighted from their carriages and bowed respectfully to the Buddha.
The Buddha bade them take their seats; the five hundred men all sat down, but Ājñāta-kaundinya alone wandered about to the left and right, subtly observing the marks of the Buddha’s countenance.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, also rose and walked alongside him; when Ājñāta-kaundinya stopped, the Buddha also stopped.
Ajātaśatru sat down, and the Buddha also sat down.
Ajātaśatru then asked the Buddha,
"By what path did you originally practice?"
"What is the purpose of shaving the hair and beard, donning the *kāṣāya*, and carrying the alms-bowl? The Buddha said,
"Since I first sought the Way, many ages have passed, beyond all calculation."
They constantly serve all Buddhas and practice the bodhisattva path; the teachers and friends they attend upon are beyond counting.
Having shaved off their hair and beards, they observe lifelong precepts, renouncing greed and attachment, and no longer indulging in finery or adornment.
One should desire that others do not desire oneself, and one should likewise not desire that others desire oneself.
The *kāṣāya* is the dharma-robe, a symbol of the ancient sages; it unties the knots of defilement so that worldly thoughts no longer arise.

The alms bowl is the appropriate vessel; it is fit for the use of those on the Way, as it disciplines the body and promotes frugality, such that one accepts nothing that is not in accordance with the Dharma.
These are all the manifestations of unconditioned purity.
"Now that I have become a Buddha and am the teacher of the world, you may follow your own inclination; do not hesitate to ask whatever you wish.
Āṭavaka said, "The master we serve is Pāyāsi;
he has been intelligent from generation to generation, his fame extends far and wide, and moreover, as one of the Brahmin caste, he is particularly superior to others."
"Although one may be as noble as a king in this world, there are those who lack benevolence; yet among my followers, there is none who does not refrain from taking life.
The Buddha said, "It was precisely because I abhorred killing that I sought the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way of a Buddha."
"You, of the Brahmin caste, merely claim to be noble through speech; though you do not kill with your hands, your minds are all intent on killing.
Now that I have become a Buddha, my body, speech, and mind are pure, and I do not kill in any way."
"Because all the people in the world delight in killing, I teach them benevolence and righteousness.
Āṣāḍha asked, "Now, the Buddha has abandoned his wife and children and cut off his own lineage; he is likely not equal to my teacher, whose descendants have continued from generation to generation."

The Buddha said: “The appearances of people in the world differ from beginning to end. All these beings were once my children in previous lives, and I too was once the child of all beings. Meetings are inevitably followed by partings; lineages are impermanent. At times, enemies follow one another as kin, and at times, relatives again become enemies. Through the conjunctions and separations of causes and conditions, all things are like an illusion.”

Parents, wives, and children are fundamentally not one's kin, nor do they belong to me; yet worldly people merely take what is "self" and "not-self" as the basis for evil deeds, thereby suffering in the future.
In a former age, I was once a Kṣatriya king named Drumāsan; I had four sons: the first was named Ugra, the second Kṣānti, the third Datta, and the fourth Sthira.

Before the king had passed away, his four sons contended for the throne. Hearing this, the king became sorrowful and anxious, thinking that as his sons contended, the people would surely be slaughtered. He immediately abdicated the kingdom and departed toward the east. As he traveled, he reflected to himself: "Human life is but brief;

only one who is free from worry lives long. Now, though I am a king, I desire to have offspring; yet once I have sons, they wish to strike one another down. If succession is such as this, what benefit does it bring to humanity?"
"I cannot bear to witness this; fearing I might kill the innocent, I shall simply leave my home to become a śramaṇa.
He then went north into the mountains and stayed in a thatched hut under the guidance of the practitioner Kapiśā.
There was also a practitioner named Māli; the King asked him about his origins:
"For what reason did you study the Way?
Māli spoke for himself:
"I married a wife but had no son; feeling ashamed before my relatives, I became a śramaṇa.
The king said, "How extraordinary!"
"I was a king with four sons; though I am not yet dead, my kingdom is in chaos because of them. Unable to bear the sight of this, I have therefore become a seeker of the Way."
Mali’s mind was thus liberated, and he subsequently applied himself with diligence.
In this way, Āṣāḍha, even if a son were virtuous, if his father were old, sick, and dying, the son could not turn back [the inevitable].
If one commits evil while alive and enters hell after death, a son cannot take their place.
For this reason, I constantly use a heart of compassion to rescue and aid all people; once I have perfected the Way and attained Buddhahood, I shall deliver and liberate the entire world.
Aśvajit said, "The Buddha is difficult to equal.

Now, in this world, there are four kinds of people: the nobleman (*kṣatriya*), the brahmin (*brāhmaṇa*), the farmer, and the artisan. Of these, we alone of the brahmin lineage are truly and nobly superior."
"The other three classes all serve my lineage.
The Buddha said,
"Suppose your lineage were truly noble, yet your wife had no son and a male child was born to a slave girl— would you raise him?"
He said, "One ought to raise them. [The other replied,] "Now,
if your grandmother has currently taken a maidservant’s son as her heir, can he truly be considered noble?"
Āṣāḍha remained silent, but his five hundred disciples all rose and said,
"How can you, Gautama Śramaṇa, disparage our clan!
Āṣāḍha is possessed of wisdom and talent, and is capable of engaging in debate."
The Buddha said:
"All remain silent.
According to your respective talents and wisdom, you shall debate it yourselves."
The Buddha questioned his ancestors three times, but there was no response.
Then the Vajrapāṇi raised his great mace and said, "The Buddha has questioned you repeatedly; for what reason do you not answer?"
Aśvajit said in fear,
"It is truly as the Buddha has spoken.
The five hundred men said:
“The Buddha’s noble wisdom is clear; as for Ambapālī, she was originally a Śākya slave-girl.
From this day forward, we request not to pay her any respect.
The Buddha said:
"Not so. In the world, there are cases where the mother is lowly but the son is noble and distinguished; Āṣāḍha is a worthy man and must not be disparaged.
If one of the Brahmin caste were to marry a Kṣatriya woman, and their son grew up, would he not study the traditions of his father’s family?"
"Should one learn from the mother's family?
They all replied,
"One should learn from the father's family."
The Buddha said, “It is so;
what harm is there in a mother being of low status?
If your son grows up to be learned in the scriptures and his conduct is lofty, surpassing that of his father, you should treat him with even greater reverence.”
If a daughter of a brahmin becomes the wife of a kṣatriya, and her son grows up knowing the excellence of his maternal family yet refuses to learn from it,
instead following his paternal family by hunting and killing living beings— would you respect him?
They all replied,
"We do not respect him.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, what is the point of questioning your mother?
Even if Āṭavaka were to have a son who was again wise, with talent so outstanding as to be peerless in the world, what would you do? They all said:
"You should take the seat of honor.
[The other replied: "Even if both parents are of the Brahma lineage, if the child born is unworthy and lacks any sense of integrity, what would you do?"
They all said, "He should sit in the lowest seat.
The Buddha said:
"In this way, is nobility something permanent?
If a son of a brahmin were to kill, steal, or violate the law, would the officials not arrest him?
He replied:
"You must capture him!
[The man replied,] "Why did you not resist and say:
'My lineage is noble; I should not be arrested and taken away'?"
He said, "Since there is currently an offense, how can you speak of 'planting' it?
The Buddha said:
"Now that I have become a Buddha, I teach the people benevolence and filial piety, instructing them with correct words to abandon desire, anger, and delusion.

Regarding those who habitually engage in evil deeds, I invariably instruct them not to kill, steal, commit sexual misconduct, speak falsely, drink intoxicants, or perform sacrifices to heterodox deities."

If a person has committed evil in the past, they must personally undergo the retribution for their crimes; to slaughter living beings by boiling them as an offering to Heaven only increases one's transgressions and provides no benefit whatsoever.
Furthermore, the Will of Heaven is pure and benevolent; how could it possibly consume human flesh?
Virtue brings about blessings; killing does not constitute merit.
Therefore, when the wise and virtuous rulers of the world hear the sutras and precepts of the Buddha, they all sever [evil] within themselves and vow not to commit wickedness.
Those who maintain the precepts at death will have their spirits ascend to the heavens;
if they can be sincere and pure in heart, they shall immediately attain the four stages of the śramaṇa:
first, the srotāpanna (stream-enterer); second, the sakṛdāgāmin (once-returner); third, the anāgāmin (non-returner); and fourth, the arhat (worthy one).
Furthermore, although the rulers of the world may wish to administer their governance with impartiality, they still demand taxes from the people and do not eliminate their greedy intentions.
Now that I have become a Buddha, I shall cause the entire world to no longer possess worldly desires, so that they may attain the Way of non-action.

Since I first sought the Way, countless kalpas have passed; in every birth I have made a vow to renounce craving and desire, to cultivate the practices of a śramaṇa, and to be without partiality toward or aversion for anyone. Among the wise and noble gentlemen of the world, there are none who, having heard the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, do not practice them accordingly; those who do not accept them will later surely come to regret it.

One who can restrain the will and is free from further craving and desire shall sever the path of birth-and-death, lamentation, and weeping; no longer pursuing mutual attachment, one attains liberation from suffering and pain.
"The world is impermanent; human beings are like bubbles on the water, arising and perishing in a single moment, unable to endure for themselves.
The Buddha asked Āṣāḍha:
"What teachings and precepts does your teacher provide?"
He replied: "The Master’s precepts forbid killing humans or oxen, stealing gold or silver, committing adultery with the Master’s family members or the wives of his disciples, and drinking alcohol."
"At forty-eight years of age, I was finally able to take a wife.
My teacher taught me to observe these eight precepts to the end.
I do not yet know the Buddha’s precepts; what further meaning do they hold?"
The Buddha said:
"Listen, you who wish to hear.
If a son of noble family comes forward to declare his intent and desires the joy of the Buddha's precepts, I shall bestow the precepts upon him according to his capacity."
Those who wish to practice the Way while remaining at home are called *upāsakas* (laymen of pure faith); they should observe the five precepts:

first, not to take pleasure in killing birds, beasts, or even crawling insects; to refrain from harming anything; to treat others as oneself and not apply blades or staves; to maintain a mind of benevolence and never utter words of killing.

Second, one must not steal: coveting the wealth of others, cheating with measures, scales, or rulers—even by the slightest fraction of a *gui* or *zhu*—one must not encroach upon others; the mind should dwell on righteousness, and the mouth must not incite taking.

Third, he does not harbor improper desires or lustfully violate women; he does not gaze upon the beauty of flowers, nor listen to fine music; his mind cultivates ritual prohibitions, and his speech does not deviate from the Dharma.
Fourth is abstaining from false speech: not slandering others by implicating them in crimes;
speaking only when the time is right; ensuring that all words are sincere and truthful;
maintaining a mind free from leakage or arrogance; and refraining from slander or praise.
Fifth, do not drink alcohol.
Even if one indulges in intoxication, let the mind have no fondness for it; let the mouth taste no flavor of it. Alcohol has thirty-six faults; do not encourage others to drink it.
"This is what is called the precept for me, the lay follower of pure faith.

The Buddha said, "I do not summon people; they come to me of their own accord to request the precepts. Out of respect, I accept them, and they propagate the teaching, abandoning evil and turning toward goodness."
Whenever those of talent and wisdom in the world wish to become śramaṇas, I always first ask them: "By what means have you attained awakening?
As a son, one ought to take filial piety and reverence as the priority, making the care and support of one's parents one's primary duty."
If one wishes to practice the Way, one must first repay one's parents.

Only after the parents have granted their permission should one explain the śramaṇa precepts to them—numbering two hundred and fifty—which require lifelong purity. One must ensure that these are not abandoned midway through failure, thereby losing the benefit of the parents' support and kindness.
If a person requests [the precepts] intentionally, their sincere resolve remains unshakable, and they are capable of upholding the laws and regulations, only then may one confer the precepts.

The precepts of a śramaṇa take compassion and benevolence as their foundation; one must not harm or kill even the smallest crawling creatures. One should cherish all people and things more than one's own infant child;
furthermore, one must not harbor resentment or lodge accusations, nor seek justice from others.
One should constantly be mindful of the kindness of one's parents and teachers and friends, striving diligently for the Way with the desire to deliver them.
A śramaṇa must not greedily deceive others or take their wealth; upon seeing various treasures, he should regard them as mere excrement or soil.

If people offer him gifts, he shall not accept them; should he accept them, he shall not keep them, but distribute them to those who are destitute. He should always preach to others the virtue of non-greed.
A śramaṇa must not have a wife or heirs; he should keep himself far from women and restrain his emotional impulses.

When walking and seeing beautiful forms, his eyes shall neither linger upon nor pursue them. Toward those who are old, he should regard them as mothers; toward others, as sisters. If his mind does not cease its desire, he should contemplate the impurities of the body to repel lustful conduct.
The arising of birth and death proceeds entirely from ignorance and craving.

A śramaṇa must not speak falsely, engage in frivolous speech, or slander others into committing offenses; he should report what he has seen or heard according to reality and must not propagate what is not righteous.
When mediating disputes, he should speak of the virtues of both parties;
his words should be deliberate and solely upright, and he must not disclose the private affairs of others.

A śramaṇa must not compose songs or verses, engage in dancing, acting, or jesting, nor discuss the performances of entertainers; he should instead apply himself diligently to profound reflection, rehearsing the old to know the new.

Whatever a śramaṇa speaks, his words must always be those of the Dharma Master; regarding what he has not heard, he must not fabricate meanings arbitrarily. He should recite the sūtras morning and night without error, practice the essentials of the Path with diligence to eliminate all defilements, and when preaching the Dharma to others, ensure his thoughts accord with its true meaning.

A śramaṇa must not lie in comfort upon fine beds; his clothing shall not be adorned with colorful patterns, his food shall not be for the sake of flavor, and he shall not use vessels of gold, silver, vermilion, or lacquer, but only bowls made of clay or iron.
A śramaṇa must not drink alcohol or crave meat, nor should he seek to savor their flavors; he must not consume medicinal wine or visit taverns.
A śramaṇa must not smear his body with various flowers or perfumes, nor burn incense upon his robes; he should instead keep his thoughts fixed on upholding the precepts.
A śramaṇa must not purchase or employ slaves, nor hire out servants or laborers; even if someone should offer them to him, he must not accept them under any circumstances.
A śramaṇa must not keep livestock, nor indulge his whims or desires by maintaining carriages, litters, or riding animals.
A śramaṇa must not store up rice or grain; he should beg for food every morning, visiting no more than seven houses.
If he receives nothing at one house, he proceeds to a second; if he receives nothing after visiting all seven houses, he should simply drink water.
When a śramaṇa enters a village, he should be like a bird that eats until full and then flies away, disregarding what remains;
even if he does not obtain food, his mind should feel no resentment.
A śramaṇa has left home and dwells without harboring attachment to security; he does not long for fine dwellings, but only for mountains, marshes, and the foot of trees.
A śramaṇa must not engage in trade or seek profit, nor should he contemplate what is noble or base among this world and that.
A śramaṇa shall not possess fields, dwellings, gardens, or orchards, nor shall he cultivate crops or take pleasure in farming.
A śramaṇa shall not discourse upon the delights of land, water, incense, or flowers; with single-minded devotion to the Way, he should not give thought to anything else.
A śramaṇa must not discuss the merits or defects of kingdoms, cities, villages, or settlements, nor judge them as superior or inferior.
A śramaṇa must not comment on the foundations of fellow practitioners, such as their fields, houses, grain, food, or clothing, noting that one person has these while another lacks them.

A śramaṇa must not engage in conversation while reclining, nor speak while eating; he must not pre-emptively concern himself with the affairs of state, the administration of armies, or the feasibility of military expeditions and conquests.
A śramaṇa must not discuss the fineness or coarseness of clothing and food, nor the excellence or defects of fine or spring water.
A śramaṇa must not speak of the physical forms of various animals as being beautiful or ugly;
such talk from this foolish person is not discourse on the Dharma.
A śramaṇa must not claim to understand the sūtras, nor speak of others' lack of understanding while boasting of his own virtue; he must not be arrogant.
When a śramaṇa expounds the Dharma, he must not say, "My sūtra is sharp while yours is obstructed," or "My observance of the precepts is pure while yours is defiled";
nor may he say, "My teacher is enlightened while yours is unenlightened.
The Buddha’s sūtras form a single unified system whose ultimate aim is non-dual; one should maintain a resolute will and remain independent, allowing neither praise nor blame to enter.
One must not say, "I am of a great clan in this world, while your lineage is humble and destitute";
nor may one say of oneself, "I have already lectured with such-and-such a person, and he is not my equal.

A śramaṇa must not disparage one another by saying, "Such-and-such a person has fine beds, desks, blankets, pillows, and bedding, while such-and-such a person has only tattered and coarse items. One must not look in a mirror or groom the beard out of a desire for smoothness and refinement.
One must not watch elders fighting, nor the fighting of lowly persons or animals;
one must not imitate them by clashing hands or fists;

one must not play with dice or gamble, nor watch or imitate various games, nor lie down indolently while scheming for food; one must not harbor thoughts of traveling to certain regions or prefectures, returning from there to here, or calculate the distances of those routes.
One must not practice as a physician for humans or animals, nor as a veterinarian for cattle or horses;
one must not instruct others to induce vomiting or purgation when they should not do so;
and one must not practice with weapons, projectiles, balls, or engage in games of throwing.

One must not study the physiognomy of men and women to discern their poverty or wealth, nobility or meanness, nor whether they possess auspicious marks; one must not study the physical characteristics of the six domestic animals;
and one must not practice divination or calculation regarding floods, droughts, calamities, or the abundance and scarcity of the harvests.

A śramaṇa must not look up at the calendar and astronomical calculations, nor deduce the movements of the sun and moon, their waxing and waning, eclipses, the falling of stars, portents and anomalies, mountain collapses, earthquakes, or the winds and rains throughout the year; he must know none of these.

The śramaṇa does not eat after midday, and though his clothing and food are coarse and simple, his mind harbors no resentment. His alms bowl is always carried beneath his left armpit; wherever he travels, he has no anxiety over hunger or cold. His body is always accompanied by the bowl, as if a bird possessed wings.

He does not consume food recklessly, and his six sense faculties are always upright. He feels shame that his will does not ascend, yet he does not resent the suffering of his body. His vow lies in the sūtras and precepts;
his eyes do not gaze upon forms, and his heart remains unmoved by what the ears, nose, mouth, or body find pleasant or unpleasant.

He regulates his diet for the sake of his body, eating neither to the point of hunger nor to satiety; when lying down, he seeks only to rest his limbs, sleeping briefly without lingering. He maintains a lofty and far-reaching resolve, constantly dwelling in *nirvāṇa*.
It is like a filial son who has lost his parents early; he wails in grief and yearns for them, never forgetting them for even a moment.

I am a śramaṇa who guards my resolve and practices the Way; when seated, I engage in meditative contemplation, and when rising, I recite the scriptures; whether awake or asleep, I am diligent, finding no leisure for anything other than the observance of the precepts.
"These are the disciples of the Buddha. The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Such precepts as these number two hundred and fifty; I have now spoken of them only in brief."
The śramaṇa restrains his mind and does not allow it to become lax; dwelling in seclusion and quietude, he eliminates lust, anger, and delusion to advance toward wisdom.

Constantly employing a mind of loving-kindness, he takes pity on the world; casting aside the habits of sleep, lethargy, and sensual desire, he single-mindedly believes in the Dharma without further doubt, and thus attains arhatship.

An Arhat is one who has already attained the state of "Thus-Come" (Arhat). It is like a person who has long been poor and burdened by debt; having managed his livelihood and gained profit, he returns home filled with joy.
Or it is like a criminal who has been imprisoned for a long time, who is skillfully released by a benevolent elder.
It is also like a slave or servant being emancipated to become a free commoner, or like one who has been ill for many years finally recovering through medical treatment;
it is also like a merchant who, after traveling through difficult and perilous paths, returns home with heavy goods.
All people rejoice at these five parables, and I, the śramaṇa, am likewise so.
I reflect that for a long time I have been bound by the five aggregates within birth and death, undergoing immeasurable further suffering, but now I have attained liberation.
What are the five aggregates?
First, form; second, sensation; third, perception; fourth, mental formations; fifth, consciousness.
These five obscure people, preventing them from seeing the Path.

The śramaṇa reflects for himself and realizes impermanence; he understands that the body is not his own and that his mind is freed from delusion. With no attachment in his heart, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is eliminated—this is the first joy.

The śramaṇa contemplates and perceives the impurity of the five internal organs within his body; his mind is freed from craving and desire, seeing neither good nor evil as dual. The aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is eliminated—this is the second joy.

The śramaṇa applies diligent reflection and sees the suffering of affectionate attachment; he does not cultivate the outflows (āsrava), and his mind is free from the pursuit of further pleasure. The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is eliminated—this is the third joy.

The śramaṇa contemplates: his body, speech, and mind are pure; he is free from further joy or anger; his mind is tranquil and settled; he neither arises nor acts; the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) has been eliminated—this is the fourth joy.

The śramaṇa reflects within himself: he has attained the Buddha’s pure transformation; all dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is severed; delusion and craving are extinguished; the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) has been eliminated—this is the fifth joy.
The Buddha told Āṣāḍha:

"My śramaṇas have cast aside all desires and practice the sutras and precepts in order to sever birth and death; thus, in this very life, they no longer harbor thoughts of grief, weeping, or mutual attachment."
I do not covet others, nor do others covet me.
Yet, through the compassion of the Way, I cherish all beings and desire to bring them across to liberation.
For one who practices the Way, there is but suffering for a single lifetime.
For those who do not practice the Way, their suffering is all the more prolonged.
It is like a person bathing; though they may achieve external cleanliness, the defilements of the mind are not removed.
One who attains arhatship eliminates all evils entirely.

The minds of ordinary people are fickle, whereas the minds of those on the Way are as one with a stone upon the earth: scorched by the sun, it does not melt; soaked by rain, it does not dissolve; blown by the wind, it does not move. Having emerged from the mundane and profane, they achieve the Ultimate Way; their minds have become cool, and there is no longer any feverish passion.
For example, it is like a lotus flower that emerges from the mud; its roots and leaves are always cool, and dust or water does not adhere to them.
A śramaṇa reflects:
"My parents raised me, and their kindness reached its limit within a single lifetime; the Buddha has opened up the world, enabling people to attain the Way."
Having personally witnessed the beginning and end of the cycle of birth and death across the five realms of existence, he knew the lifespans of others, and his will was already rectified.
Whatever he did with ease, if he wished to ascend to heaven, he ascended; if he wished to enter the sea, he entered.
It is like bathing a corpse with fragrant perfumes; the perfume cannot permeate it. Likewise, teaching a wicked person to do good does not guarantee they will become good.
When a person’s mind is evil, both their body and speech are likewise evil.
The words of the non-Buddhist scholars are merely indulgence; they possess no true Way.
When a practitioner of the Way hears this, he should ultimately not respond.

He knows that the intentions and perceptions of ordinary people are all inverted; being ignorant and unable to understand the Way, they mistake the correct for the false and cannot distinguish between the true and the counterfeit.

Because the Sages take pity on them, they bestow upon them compassion and love; the śramaṇa maintains his mind just as a person wearing new clothes is careful and protective in sitting and rising, not wishing to stain or soil them.
Therefore, one who upholds the precepts constantly contends with the mind, ensuring that even if a hundred evils should come, they shall never be accepted.
When parents give birth to a child, they should transform them with the Way while young; if the child commits crimes and dies when grown, the parents cannot hold their kin responsible.
For example, if one sits upon a bench made of wood but lacking ropes, one cannot remain seated.
Likewise, a disciple who lacks a wise teacher cannot attain the Way; such is the case with these Confucian scholars.
In my previous lives, I served many sages and saints, and what I received was not ordinary; yet none of them acted as my teachers.

Those who have attained Arhatship can declare for themselves: "In such-and-such a place I attained the stage of Stream-enterer; in such-and-such a place I attained the stage of Once-returner and Non-returner, up to the state of Arhatship, which is total liberation, no longer subject to birth and death."
He possesses thorough knowledge of their breadth and narrowness, like one who, in viewing a fine painting, distinguishes its five colors.
He beholds all people in the world as possessing the states of the three poisons, arrogance, negligence, and craving for sensory flavors.
Knowing for himself that he had attained liberation, he no longer craved rebirth in the heavens nor took pleasure in the human realm;
he thought only of sentient beings, desiring to bring them to liberation.

Those ordinary people who have not yet heard this should receive and study it with careful attention, just as when one holds a colored thread through lapis lazuli beads, and all five colors appear clearly.

With the eye of the Way, one perceives where the spirits and souls of people have come from when they are born, and to which realm they proceed when they die; one knows that such-and-such a person, upon death, has fallen into hell; some have fallen among the animals; some have fallen among the ghosts and spirits; some have entered human form; and some, upon death, have ascended to heaven.

Having realized the Way for myself, I have severed these five attachments; having already attained what I sought, I regard my body as mere earth. You may take my body and break it into pieces if you wish.
By this, one clarifies the true from the false, just as when entering clear water, all that is present—gravel, pebbles, and precious jewels—is seen.
One foreknows the world, perceiving the hundred as one and the one as the hundred.
Why is this so? Suppose one person gives birth to a child, and through successive generations down to a great-grandson, the lineage flourishes to a hundred members.

Yet at some point, those hundred people may die and the family line becomes empty; however, there remains a single śramaṇa who has attained the Way, who clearly perceives both good and evil, and knows which of the deceased will be reborn in a good realm and which will fall into an evil realm.
One perceives within one's own body the proportions of the four elements and thereby knows the lifespan, suffering, joy, and duration of others.

Originally arising from ignorance, mental consciousness constitutes volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); from these formations, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises. Thus, through the convergence of causes and conditions, one is entrusted to the mother’s womb; there, they harbor mutual anxieties and concerns—parents say, "This is my child," and the child says, "These are my parents"—yet as the spirit transmigrates, none recognize their true selves.
Those who were virtuous in their past lives are reborn as humans and are wealthy, noble, and long-lived;
those who were not virtuous suffer from short lifespans—each according to their original karma.
Heaven, earth, people, and things all rely upon the four elements:
first, earth; second, water; third, fire; and fourth, wind.

Within the human body, that which is solid is earth, that which is moist and supple is water, that which is warm and hot is fire, and that which is the movement of breath is wind. One borrows these for life, but at death they return to their source. When one calculates their beginning and end, each is distinct from the other, yet ordinary people do not perceive this.
Between heaven and earth, those who live are like a dream; their lifespans and fortunes are exceedingly brief, and they die amidst a state of constant turmoil.
It is like the wind blowing over the ocean, where waves chase one another; so it is with birth and death, coming and going without rest.

The śramaṇa who has attained the Way fully knows the formation and destruction, the beginning and end, of heaven and earth, as well as all events within a single kalpa and the successive lives through which his own body has passed.

He also knows the affairs of incalculable kalpas in the distant past; thus he knows that among the immortals and transcendents throughout the world who have attained the Way, none can equal the Buddha.

I know that my own will was originally manifold, yet now it has been unified into one; I constantly grieve for the multitudes whose chests are muddled and disordered by the intoxication of greed, desire, delusion, lust, anger, and ignorance, such that they may harbor affection and love while remaining ignorant of this essential truth.
Having attained the Way, his vision reaches everywhere.
Like a person looking into a mirror, he flies through the air without obstruction, passing through stone walls as if they were nothing.
He can ascend Mount Sumeru and reach out his hand to touch the sun and moon.
He can cause water and fire to emerge separately from within his body;
he can submerge into the earth and emerge from one side;
and he can travel through the air, sitting or lying down at will.
It can cause even the Māras, Brahmās, Śakras, and all the devas to bow down in submission.
It is like a potter who, having fired his earthenware vessels, makes them so that they hold water without leaking.
Ordinary people are like unbaked clay forms; those who have attained the Way are like the fired vessels—whether dry or wet, and even when submerged in water, they do not break.
Just as a goldsmith may fashion any vessel he desires, so too is it with one who has attained supernormal power (*ṛddhi*): they can manifest whatever transformation they wish.
In the workshop of a smith, the intense fire melts the metal to form the vessels.
I, a śramaṇa, have likewise attained the Way through the cultivation of the mind.
It is like a dry cowhide: when rolled up it makes a sound, and when stretched out it also makes a sound; yet if moistened with fat and grease, it becomes supple whether rolled or stretched.
Such is the mind set on the Way: all things become soft and pliant, and there is no longer any rigidity or hardness.
It is like being on a high tower and seeing and hearing the singing, dancing, bells, drums, and the sounds of various domestic animals of those below;
the ear of the Path is likewise, for it hears both the music of the heavens and the cries of hunger, thirst, and pain from the hungry ghosts and the hells.

He possesses the insight to discern the minds of others: those with lustful dispositions and those without; those with various states of joy, anger, hatred, or love; the foolish and the wise; the strong and the weak; those easy to transform and those difficult to transform; and those who delight in the Path and those who do not. He distinguishes and knows them all, just as a person who delights in bathing and rubbing their body ensures that no part is left untouched by thoroughly and repeatedly massaging it.
With the eye of the Way, he observes and knows those who may be saved; he then takes up the Buddhist scriptures, explains them, and bestows them upon them.
Those whose wills are good shall again become human beings;
those whose conduct is slightly superior shall, upon death, ascend to heaven.
If one maintains pure precepts, one will attain the four paths of the śramaṇa.
Those who have attained these paths all know the affairs of one lifetime, ten lifetimes, a hundred lifetimes, and countless lifetimes.

He also knows the beginning and end of heaven and earth, and the times of the formation and destruction of kalpas; he knows from where his bodies have arisen throughout countless kalpas, being born at various times with different parents, names, and surnames, and varying in the length of their lifespans.

He knows that at those times, one may ascend from the human path to become a deva, or descend from the deva path to become a human; or one may enter hell from the human realm, or become an animal or a hungry ghost from hell; or emerge as a human from the realm of hungry ghosts; or from a human become a spirit or ghost, or enter hell from the realm of spirits and ghosts, or ascend to become a deva—all these he discerns and understands through his own contemplation.

It is like a person who, being a long-distance traveler, remembers their hometown and possesses full knowledge of it; they observe the five realms of existence and know for themselves that they have attained liberation.
With mastery over the power of the Path, whether they wish to live for a hundred years, a thousand years, ten thousand years, or even up to incalculable kalpas, they are able to do so.
If one wishes not to eat for ten days, a hundred days, a year, or a hundred years—even up to an incalculable number of years—one may do so; yet if one wishes to eat, one eats immediately.
It is like ascending a high tower to listen to and observe the voices of people below as they sit or stand, speaking in the east, west, south, or north.

All who hear and see this know that the practitioner has realized for himself that his will is already pure and he has abandoned both good and evil. It is like a man who, having committed a transgression against the law, is forced by the officials to parade about with a dead dog hung around his neck; filled with shame and humiliation, he desires only to be quickly released from it.
Those who have attained arhatship feel such shame regarding their bodies.
There are two classes of arhats:
one class is for the sake of cessation, and one class is for the sake of protection.
What is called "extinction" (nirodha) refers to one who, being concerned for their own attainment of the Way, immediately enters nirvana;
what is called "protection" (anurakṣaṇā) refers to one who is concerned for others, delivering and liberating all under heaven.

It is like clear water, wherein the sand, stones, fish, and turtles naturally appear; once the mind of the Way is purified, one perceives everything within the mental consciousnesses of all under heaven.
“The śramaṇa is like this.
Is your teacher’s instruction capable of such a thing? Aśva replied:
"This is indeed difficult to fathom.
The Buddha said, "In the world,
I also see practitioners of the Way who, though ignorant of the Buddha-dharma, dwell in seclusion within marshes and swamps, subsisting on fruits and gourds, and say:"
"If one does not rely on a teacher, one shall attain spontaneity (*svayambhū*).
Is this the attainment of the Way? He replied:
"No," the Buddha said, "the Way is attained through the mind; there must be the Dharma of a teacher."
This is the first instance of deluded folly in believing in the Way.

Furthermore, there are Daoist practitioners who gather the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a hundred herbs, consuming them as medicinal prescriptions, believing that by their own efforts they may attain transcendence.
"Do your teacher's disciples also believe this? He replied, "They do not."
"This is the second type of delusion: those who believe in the Way [of the heretics].

There may be practitioners who abandon their parents, wear deerskin robes, sleep upon straw mats, let their hair grow wild, and abstain from food; they prostrate to the heavens seeking the Way, only to suffer hardships in vain without achieving anything."
"Do you emulate this? He replied, "I do not."
"This is the third way of deluded and false belief in the Way.

There are also practitioners who dwell in secluded places, inscribe 'The Way' above their gates, and perform sacrifices to water, fire, the sun, the moon, and the five planets; they slaughter animals by boiling them to offer to Heaven, and seek blessings through such extensive rites."
"Did you do this? He replied, "I did not."
"This is called the fourth deluded and false path of belief. The Buddha told Āḍa:

"Since the beginning of heaven and earth, there have been twenty-three great brahmin practitioners, namely: Kīrti, Rāma, Jina, Kāśyapa, Aruṇa, Kacchapa, Gopaka, Acala, Jvālāmukha, Pāṭaliputra, Govinda, Alarka, Gautama, Śikhaṇḍin, Gopāla, Kāśyapa, Vatsapra, Abhaya, Bṛhaspati, Uccāṅga, Parileya, Khara, and Bhṛgu. All the cities and towns in the world were created by these twenty-three men together."
"Now, how does this Vakkula compare to such people as these?
He replied, "He is not their equal."
The Buddha asked,
"What excellence does your teacher possess that he can serve as a teacher to emperors and kings, enabling them to attain the Way? He replied:
"No. [The Buddha asked:
"Are you able to act as teachers for the prince, the great ministers, and the high officials, enabling them to attain the Way?
They replied:
"No. "Is your teacher able to instruct the men and women—whether old, middle-aged, or young—and cause you all to attain the Way?"
He replied, “I cannot. [The Buddha asked,] “Has your teacher’s ancestor attained the Way?”
He replied, “I have not heard the Teacher’s instruction.
[The Buddha asked,] “Which path do you follow?”
He said, "The teacher says that those who observe the eight precepts will ascend to the Brahma Heaven upon death.
[The Buddha asked,] "Have you ever seen anyone like yourselves who, having observed these eight precepts, ascended to the Brahma Heaven?"
He replied, "I have merely heard the words of my teacher.
The Buddha told Āṣāḍha:

“I, a śramaṇa who has attained arhatship, know the births and deaths within kalpas; I distinguish that at such-and-such a time various people were this person or became that person from such-and-such a state. I know the affairs of the people of the world as well as those of the heavens.
I can fly to wherever I wish to go; I can appear and vanish at will; I can shake heaven and earth and move Mount Sumeru;

I can enter and exit the Avīci hell and transform things according to my will. When parents die, I know into which realm they have fallen; I seek them out and provide guidance, enabling them to attain liberation. If a child attains the Way, both parents are delivered.”
"Furthermore, I, a śramaṇa, maintain a single right intention and practice the two hundred and fifty precepts, proceeding toward the path of unconditioned nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Āṣāḍha:

"I abandoned my kingdom and renounced kingship to become a śramaṇa, seeking to sever the cycle of birth and death. Now I have attained spontaneity, becoming a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat. I serve as the teacher for all that is above and below heaven; those who uphold my sūtras and precepts shall none fail to attain the Way."
I constantly maintain a heart of loving-kindness to transform the world, leading people away from evil and toward goodness.

Goodness can be practiced forever, whereas evil cannot endure for long; suffering may be dwelt upon for a long time, but pleasure cannot be preserved. Pleasure brings momentary satisfaction, yet after a while one suffers; when retribution arrives and regret ensues, it will be too late to do anything about it.
Thereupon, Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya gazed intently at the Buddha’s body and thought to himself:
"The Buddha possesses thirty-two marks; why is it that I do not see even a single one of them?"

The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately extended his tongue; he first licked his left ear, then licked his right ear, and again licked the hairline. He covered his face with his tongue and then slowly withdrew it.
Āṣāḍha sighed and said, "One such as the Buddha is difficult to encounter; only once in ten thousand ages does one possess a tongue-mark such as this—how could I not know [of his greatness]?
The Buddha said:
"You have been gone for a long time; go and offer your thanks to your teacher.
The five hundred men all stepped forward, touched the Buddha's feet, and departed.
Vīkaśa was traveling in a carriage when he saw his disciples approaching; he stopped immediately to wait for them. When the disciples arrived, he descended from the carriage and paid his respects.
The Master said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is renowned throughout the world; does he possess the marks [of a great man]?
Why has he stayed so long, and what matters did he exhaustively discuss?"
Āṣāḍha said, "What was spoken this morning was entirely without error; once we have returned home and finished our meal, I shall explain it to you at leisure.
The teacher said:
“Did the Buddha not allow you to remain for a meal?
He replied, “The Buddha was sitting beneath a tree with nothing at all; knowing it was time for a meal, he sent me back, and so we returned together.”
After the meal was finished, Aśvajit approached his teacher and recounted the Buddha’s words in full.
The teacher said, "In recounting the Buddha’s words, you have neither added nor subtracted anything; do you wish for me to serve him?"
Āḍa said, "I have listened to what the Buddha has spoken; he has surpassed us brahmins. I only fear that my own kind will be unable to serve him.
His teacher then became enraged, stamped his foot upon the ground, and said:
"I have been your teacher for many lifetimes; why am I now inferior?
Āṭavaka replied, "Teacher, please go there yourself and observe his wisdom and capability."
The teacher said, "Very well,
you should personally invite the Buddha to converse with him. That evening,
he immediately prepared beds and mats and provided provisions for five hundred people.
At cockcrow, the teacher arrived in person and announced his name. The Buddha invited him to meet; after he had performed his prostrations and sat down to one side, he joined his palms and said:
"I have now prepared a modest meal; I pray that the Buddha, together with the assembly of śramaṇas, will condescend to show your majestic presence."
The Buddha signaled his consent by remaining silent. Pukkasāti was filled with joy; he took his leave and returned to prepare the meal.
Before noon had passed, he sent Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya again to go and welcome him.

The Buddha, together with five hundred śramaṇas, proceeded to the house. Once they were seated, the meal was served; when the food had been distributed and the water for washing hands was finished, Pukkasāti asked the Buddha:
"Yesterday, when Ābhya returned, he spoke on the road about the Buddha's words. I did not hear them clearly; I wish to hear them again."
The Buddha said,
"All of these are without increase or decrease.
He then further recounted what he had spoken yesterday.
Hearing the Buddha’s words, he was filled with joy and immediately prostrated himself,
saying, "Yesterday, for no reason, I became angry at what Ājñātakauṇḍinya said. The Buddha said:
“Although you were angry, you are a worthy disciple, like a fine horse that understands the mind and intentions of its master.
The Buddha then offered a blessing to Āṣāḍha, saying:
“May you have a long life and remain free from illness.”
Thereupon the teacher praised the Buddha, saying:
"Fire can illuminate the darkness; The ocean and rivers are kings over the hundred valleys.
The Sage’s vast instruction Is like a land possessing an enlightened ruler."
"The maṇi jewel is foremost; the moon is the brightest among the stars.
As the sun illuminates the world beneath it, so too is the Buddha alone the Honored One within the three realms.
Knowing that his mind was supple, upright, and free from evil, the Buddha spoke these verses for him:
"A person should practice benevolence and righteousness, giving alms to create merit;
they should realize that sensory consciousness is not the ultimate goal and maintain their conduct according to the sutras and precepts.
This world is perilous, where pleasure is scarce and suffering is abundant."
One should be concerned for one's own person and must not be indolent;
one should strive to sever greed and desire, which lead to the habit of fear and the pain of lamentation and weeping caused by birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"The separation from those one loves is suffering; all such things are suffering.
Therefore, the sages seek the Way of the Unconditioned.
Vīkaśa’s mind was liberated; he rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and with tears falling, said:
"I recall my ancestors, none of whom ever knew the Buddha.
I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me.
I have brothers, a wife, children, and various kinsmen whom I now wish to bring here so that they may receive the Buddha-dharma."
The Buddha said, "You may.
They immediately came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, received the three refuges, and together with Āṣāḍha and the others, all observed the five precepts.
Later, when Vakkula passed away,
his disciples asked the Buddha,
"As for this teacher who has died, to which realm has he gone?"
The Buddha said:
"They have already attained the third fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmin) and will be reborn among the Anāgāmins of the nineteenth heaven; they shall attain parinirvāṇa there.
To Ābhya and the five hundred others who wished to become śramaṇas, the Buddha said:
"Return each to your own home, maintain the five precepts well, and only when your resolve is firm may you leave the household life.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, they were all greatly rejoiced; they paid their respects and departed.
The Scripture on the Buddha’s Explanation for the Brahmin Āṣāḍha.
